Part 1 — Essential Concepts

Plain-language explanations of the four syllabus sections. Each concept is self-contained: you can read this part without opening the original question bank.

A.Query Processing & Optimization

Definition — Query processing

The steps a DBMS performs to turn an SQL statement into a result: parsing → validation → relational-algebra translation → optimization (choose the cheapest plan) → code generation → execution. The optimizer is the part that matters for this unit.

1. Query trees

A query tree (expression tree / evaluation tree) is a diagram of a relational-algebra expression. Leaves are base relations, internal nodes are operators (σ selection, π projection, ⋈ join, × Cartesian product), and the root produces the final result. Data flows bottom-up; each node's output is the next node's input.

The initial (canonical) tree is a literal translation of the SQL: Cartesian products first, then one big selection, then a projection at the top. It is correct but almost never efficient. The optimized tree is the same expression rewritten by heuristic rules so that small intermediate results are produced as early as possible.

2. Heuristic (rule-based) optimization — the standard step sequence

  1. Break up conjunctive selections: σ(c1 ∧ c2) becomes σc1(σc2(R)) — a cascade.
  2. Push selections down the tree as far as the conditions allow (toward the leaves).
  3. Replace Cartesian products + selection by joins: σR.a=S.b(R × S) ⇒ R ⋈a=b S.
  4. Order the joins so the most selective (smallest-result) join runs first.
  5. Push projections down to keep only the attributes needed above (reduces tuple width and block count).
  6. Combine cascaded selections/projections into a single operation where possible.
Key idea

Every heuristic step preserves the result set but changes the cost. The goal is always the same: make the intermediate relations as small as possible as early as possible.

3. Which conditions can be pushed where

Condition typeExampleCan be pushed?
Single-relatione.dept_id = 3Yes — push onto that relation's leaf.
Join conditione.emp_id = w.emp_idYes — becomes the join predicate.
Mixed (spans two relations, non-equality)w.hours*400 > e.salaryNo — applied immediately after the join.

Missing this distinction is a classic exam error: a mixed condition cannot be pushed below the join that supplies both of its relations.

4. Cost-based optimization

When several equivalent plans survive the heuristics, the optimizer estimates each plan's cost using catalog statistics (tuple counts, block counts, blocking factor, index heights, distinct values) and picks the cheapest. Cost is usually measured in block (page) I/O, sometimes with CPU cost added.

Definition — Selectivity

Selectivity = the fraction of tuples that satisfy a predicate. A predicate with selectivity 0.1 keeps 10 % of the rows. The result cardinality = (input tuples) × (selectivity). With several independent conditions, multiply the selectivities.

5. Access paths and indexes

For a single-table selection the optimizer chooses between:

  • Linear (full) scan — read every block of the relation.
  • Clustered index — records of a key value are stored physically together, so a range reads few blocks.
  • Secondary (unclustered) index — each matching record can sit in a different block: roughly one I/O per record.
  • Covering index — the index alone holds all needed columns, so the table is never touched.

A sargable predicate lets the index be used for a range seek. Wrapping the indexed column in a function (DATE_FORMAT(hire_date,...), TO_CHAR(...)) destroys sargability and forces a scan — the classic slow-report bug.

6. Join ordering

Joins are commutative and associative, so the same query has many join orders. The optimizer estimates each order's intermediate sizes and picks the one with the smallest total. A plan that forms a Cartesian product early is almost always the worst.

B.Transaction Processing

Definition — Transaction

A transaction is a logical unit of work: a sequence of operations that must be treated as a single, indivisible action. It ends with COMMIT (make permanent) or ROLLBACK (undo everything).

1. The ACID properties

PropertyMeaningHow the unit demonstrates it
AtomicityAll operations happen, or none do.A failed debit triggers ROLLBACK; a transfer never half-completes.
ConsistencyA transaction moves the database from one valid state to another.A CHECK constraint rejects a negative balance.
IsolationConcurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work.Two-session exercises: snapshots, dirty reads, lost updates.
DurabilityCommitted changes survive a crash.Write-ahead logging; REDO of committed work.

2. Transaction control statements

  • START TRANSACTION (MySQL) / first DML (Oracle) — begins a transaction.
  • COMMIT — makes all changes permanent and releases locks.
  • ROLLBACK — undoes all changes since the transaction began.
  • SAVEPOINT name / ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name — partial rollback: undo only back to the marker.
Trap — DDL commits implicitly

In both MySQL and Oracle, a DDL statement (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) commits the current transaction implicitly. A later ROLLBACK has nothing left to undo. This is why “I rolled back but the change stayed” happens after an ALTER.

3. Isolation levels and the anomalies they permit

LevelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantom
READ UNCOMMITTEDPossiblePossiblePossible
READ COMMITTED (Oracle default)NoPossiblePossible
REPEATABLE READ (MySQL default)NoNoPossible*
SERIALIZABLENoNoNo

* InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ blocks the phantom for the same snapshot via next-key/gap locking; a non-locking read still returns the snapshot count, while a locking read sees the current data.

Definitions — the three anomalies
  • Dirty read — reading data written by another transaction that has not yet committed.
  • Non-repeatable read — the same row returns different values when read twice in one transaction.
  • Phantom — re-running the same query returns new rows inserted by another transaction.

4. The lost-update problem

Two transactions read the same value, each computes a new value from it, and both write back. The second write overwrites the first, so one update is lost. The cure is to lock the row while it is read: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (exclusive) so the second transaction blocks until the first commits.

5. Autocommit

When autocommit = 1 (MySQL default), every statement commits immediately, so a lone ROLLBACK does nothing. START TRANSACTION suspends autocommit for the duration of that one transaction, which is why the rollback then works. Oracle's SET AUTOCOMMIT ON/OFF is a client setting, not a database one.

C.Concurrency Control

1. Schedules and notation

A schedule is an interleaving of the operations of several transactions, read left to right in time order. Notation: r1(A) = T1 reads A; w1(A) = T1 writes A; c1 = T1 commits; a1 = T1 aborts. Two operations conflict if they belong to different transactions, access the same item, and at least one is a write. Read/read pairs never conflict.

2. Conflict serializability and precedence graphs

Build a precedence graph: a node per transaction, and an edge Ti → Tj whenever an operation of Ti precedes a conflicting operation of Tj. The schedule is conflict serializable iff the graph is acyclic. A topological order of the graph is an equivalent serial order.

Definition — View serializability

A schedule is view serializable if it is view-equivalent to some serial schedule: the same transaction reads each item's initial value, every read reads from the same write, and the same transaction performs each item's final write. Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable, but not the reverse — the gap is closed by blind writes (a write not preceded by a read of that item in the same transaction).

3. Recoverability classes

ClassConditionPrevents
RecoverableIf Tj reads from Ti, then ci must come before cj.Committing a transaction whose input was rolled back.
Cascadeless (avoids cascading rollback)Every read is of a value written by a committed transaction.A chain of rollbacks when one transaction aborts.
StrictNo transaction reads or writes an item until the last writer of that item has committed or aborted.Dirty reads and cascading rollback; also simplifies recovery.

Strict ⇒ cascadeless ⇒ recoverable. The implications do not run the other way.

4. Lock-based concurrency control

  • Shared lock S(X) — read access; several transactions may hold S on the same item.
  • Exclusive lock X(X) — write access; held by exactly one transaction.
  • Compatibility: S/S compatible; S/X and X/X conflict. A conflicting request blocks.
Held \ RequestedSX
SGrantedBlocked
XBlockedBlocked

5. Two-phase locking (2PL)

A transaction has a growing phase (only acquiring locks) and a shrinking phase (only releasing). The moment it holds all its locks and begins releasing is the lock point. Plain 2PL guarantees conflict serializability but not recoverability. Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until commit/abort — that guarantees both serializability and strictness, and is what real engines implement.

Trap — 2PL vs strict 2PL

A transaction that releases a lock before commit satisfies 2PL but not strict 2PL (e.g. X(A) … U(A) … c). Releasing a shared lock early is allowed by both; releasing an exclusive lock early breaks strictness only.

6. Deadlock

A deadlock is a cycle in the wait-for graph (edge Ti → Tj when Ti waits for a lock held by Tj). Handled by:

  • Detection + recovery — detect the cycle and abort a victim (usually the youngest, or the lowest rollback cost).
  • Prevention by timestamp — Wait-Die: older requester waits, younger requester dies. Wound-Wait: older requester wounds (aborts) the younger holder, younger requester waits.
  • Timeout — a blocked request gives up after a fixed wait (MySQL innodb_lock_wait_timeout).

7. Timestamp ordering (TO)

Each transaction gets a timestamp TS(T). Each item X keeps R-TS(X) (largest timestamp of a reader) and W-TS(X) (largest timestamp of a writer). Operations run only if they arrive in timestamp order; otherwise the transaction aborts and restarts with a new timestamp. No locks, so no deadlock — but possibly many restarts.

Thomas Write Rule

A refinement: if TS(T) < W-TS(X) but TS(T) ≥ R-TS(X), the write is obsolete — ignore it and continue instead of aborting. It changes only the stale blind-write case and makes some non-serializable schedules acceptable.

8. Optimistic concurrency control (validation)

Transactions run freely in a read phase, then pass a validation phase before writing. Each transaction has a ReadSet and WriteSet. Tj validates against every earlier-validated Ti: it passes if either finish(Ti) < start(Tj), or start(Tj) < finish(Ti) < validation(Tj) and WriteSet(Ti) ∩ ReadSet(Tj) = ∅. Otherwise it aborts.

D.Database Recovery

1. Failures

  • Transaction failure — a bad statement or explicit ROLLBACK. The engine undoes the transaction; the database stays available.
  • System failure (crash) — power loss or software crash. Volatile memory is lost; the log on disk survives.
  • Media failure — disk damage; needs a backup restore plus log replay.

2. The log and write-ahead logging

A log is an append-only record of every change. Write-ahead logging (WAL) is the rule that the log record for a change must reach stable storage before the changed page is written to disk. This is what makes recovery possible: the log can always reconstruct or undo a change.

Log recordMeaning
<T,start> / <T,commit>Transaction begins / commits
<T,X,new>Deferred-modification write record (new value only)
<T,X,old,new>Immediate-modification write record
<T,X,old>UNDO-only write record
<T,X,V> during rollbackRedo-only compensation record
<checkpoint {list}>Checkpoint; list = active transactions
<T,abort>Rollback complete (all old values already restored)

3. The four update strategies

StrategyWhen data reaches diskRecovery action
DeferredOnly after commitREDO committed transactions only (forward scan, log order). No UNDO.
ImmediateAny time (even uncommitted)UNDO uncommitted (backward), then REDO committed (forward).
UNDO-onlyEvery write forced before its commit recordUNDO uncommitted only (backward).
Shadow pagingCommit switches a root pointerNo log: use whichever page table the root designates.
The two recovery passes (immediate modification)

Pass 1 — UNDO: scan the log backward; for every transaction with a start but no commit/abort, restore each item's old value. Pass 2 — REDO: scan forward; for every committed transaction, re-apply each new value in log order. UNDO must go backward so the earliest old value wins.

4. Checkpoints

At a checkpoint, all log records and all modified pages are forced to disk. Benefits:

  • A transaction that committed before the checkpoint needs no recovery action.
  • Recovery only has to scan the log from the earliest start of a transaction active at the checkpoint onward.
  • Under deferred modification, a transaction active at the checkpoint that later commits must still be redone from its first write, because nothing of it was on disk.

5. Shadow paging

The database keeps two page tables: the current table (for the active transaction) and the shadow table (the committed state). A modified page is copied to a new location, and the current table is updated. Commit makes the current table the shadow table (one atomic pointer switch). A crash before commit simply discards the current table — no undo is needed. The cost is that committed data ends up scattered and needs periodic garbage collection.

Trap — recovery order and direction
  • UNDO is always backward (latest log entry first). Running it forward leaves the wrong value.
  • REDO is always forward in log order, so the last write to an item wins.
  • A transaction with an abort record is already complete: neither undo nor redo it.
  • UNDO and REDO write absolute values, so repeating them is harmless (idempotent).

Part 2 — Important Formulas & Rules

Every formula the unit uses, with its variables and a short worked example. Statistics used in the manual problems: EMP = 50,000 tuples / 1,250 blocks / blocking factor 40; DEPT = 10 tuples / 1 block; WORKS = 150,000 tuples / 3,000 blocks; PROJ = 200 tuples.

1.Cost & Cardinality Models

1.1 Block count of a relation

bR = ⌈ nR / bfR ⌉   where   bfR = ⌊ B / tR ⌋

nR = number of tuples · B = block size (bytes) · tR = tuple size (bytes) · bfR = blocking factor (tuples per block) · bR = number of blocks.

Worked example (U3-A-04): B = 4,000 B. EMP tuples are 100 B → bf = ⌊4000/100⌋ = 40, so bEMP = 50,000 / 40 = 1,250 blocks. A projected temp relation of 40 B/tuple → bf = 100 → 50,000/100 = 500 blocks (a saving of 750 blocks, 60 %).

1.2 Selectivity and result cardinality

|result| = nR × s1 × s2 × …   (independent conditions)

si = selectivity (fraction of tuples satisfying condition i).

Worked example (U3-A-03): σsalary>50000(EMP) with s = 0.6 → 50,000 × 0.6 = 30,000 tuples. σcity='Pune'(DEPT) → 2 of 10 → 2 tuples. The join then keeps 30,000 × (2/10) = 6,000 tuples.

1.3 Join cardinality estimate

|R ⋈ S| ≈ ( nR × nS ) / max( V(R,a), V(S,a) )

V(R,a) = number of distinct values of the join attribute a in R.

Worked example (U3-A-05): EMP(50,000) ⋈ WORKS(150,000) on emp_id; each EMP row matches 3 WORKS rows → 50,000 × 3 = 150,000 tuples.

2.Join Algorithms & Index Access Costs

2.1 Block Nested-Loop Join (BNL)

CostBNL = bouter + ⌈ bouter / (M − 2) ⌉ × binner

M = number of buffer pages available · bouter, binner = block counts of the outer and inner relations. The inner relation is re-scanned once per outer chunk of (M−2) blocks, so the smaller relation should normally be the outer one.

Worked example (U3-A-07): M = 52, so M − 2 = 50.
(i) EMP outer: 1,250 + ⌈1250/50⌉ × 3,000 = 1,250 + 25 × 3,000 = 76,250.
(ii) WORKS outer: 3,000 + ⌈3000/50⌉ × 1,250 = 3,000 + 60 × 1,250 = 78,000.
Winner: (i), EMP as the outer relation.

2.2 Index Nested-Loop Join

CostINL = bouter + nouter × ( h + k )

h = height of the index on the inner join attribute · k = block I/Os per matching inner tuple (≈ 1 if unclustered, ≈ 1/bf if clustered).

Worked example (U3-A-07): index height 3, each EMP tuple matches 3 WORKS tuples at 1 I/O each: 1,250 + 50,000 × (3 + 3) = 301,250. It loses to BNL because every outer tuple triggers an index probe on unclustered matches.

2.3 Access-path costs for a single-table selection

PathCost (blocks)Notes
Linear scanbRAlways available.
Clustered indexh + ⌈r / bf⌉r = number of matching records.
Secondary indexh + r≈ one I/O per matching record (unclustered).

h = index height · r = matching records · bf = blocking factor.

Worked example (U3-A-08): r = 5,000, h = 3, bf = 40, bEMP = 1,250.
Linear scan = 1,250. Secondary = 3 + 5,000 = 5,003. Clustered = 3 + ⌈5000/40⌉ = 3 + 125 = 128.
Ranking: clustered < scan < secondary. Break-even where the scan beats the secondary index: 3 + r = 1,250 → r = 1,247 records. Above that the scan is cheaper.

2.4 Pushdown savings

Reduction factor = (sum of intermediate sizes, unoptimized) / (sum of intermediate sizes, optimized)
Worked example (U3-A-03): initial tree forms EMP × DEPT = 500,000 tuples before selecting. Optimized tree's intermediates total 30,000 + 2 + 6,000 = 36,002. Comparing the product with the two selected inputs: 500,000 / 30,002 ≈ 16.7× reduction.

3.Schedule Classes & Serializability

3.1 Conflict and conflict equivalence

Rule

Two operations conflict iff they are from different transactions, access the same item, and at least one is a write. Two schedules are conflict equivalent if they order every conflicting pair the same way.

Worked example (U3-C-01): S1 = r1(A) w2(A) r2(B) w1(B) r3(A) w3(B). Conflicting pairs: (r1(A),w2(A)), (w2(A),r3(A)), (r2(B),w1(B)), (r2(B),w3(B)), (w1(B),w3(B)) → 5 pairs. The pair (r1(A),r3(A)) is read/read, so it does not conflict.

3.2 Conflict serializability test

  1. Draw one node per transaction.
  2. For every conflicting pair, add an edge from the earlier transaction to the later one.
  3. Acyclic ⇒ conflict serializable; a topological order is an equivalent serial order.
  4. Cycle ⇒ not conflict serializable.

3.3 View serializability requirements

  • Initial read: if Ti reads the initial value of X in S, it does so in the serial order too.
  • Read-from: if Tj reads a value written by Ti in S, it does so in the serial order too.
  • Final write: the transaction performing the last write of X in S does so in the serial order too.
Worked example (U3-C-05, S5a): r1(A) w2(A) w1(A) w3(A) has the cycle T1→T2→T1, so it is not conflict serializable. View test: r1 reads the initial value (so T1 first) and T3 makes the final write (so T3 last). Only the order T1, T2, T3 satisfies both — it is view serializable.

3.4 Recoverability, cascadelessness, strictness

ClassFormal conditionTest on a schedule
RecoverableIf Tj reads from Ti, then ci < cj.Find every read-from pair; check commit order.
CascadelessEvery read is of a committed value: no read of an uncommitted write.Every rj(X) must follow the writer's commit.
StrictNo read or write of X until the last writer of X has committed/aborted.Also forbids overwriting an uncommitted value.
Worked example (U3-C-07): R2 = w1(A) r2(A) c2 c1 → not recoverable (T2 reads from T1 but c2 precedes c1). R4 = w1(A) w2(A) c1 c2 → recoverable and cascadeless (no reads) but not strict (T2 overwrites T1's uncommitted A).

4.Locking, 2PL & Deadlock

4.1 Lock compatibility

Held \ RequestedSX
SGrantedBlocked
XBlockedBlocked

4.2 Two-phase locking rules

  • Growing phase: a transaction may only acquire locks (and may upgrade S → X).
  • Shrinking phase: a transaction may only release locks.
  • Lock point: the instant the transaction holds its final lock, i.e. the boundary between the two phases.
  • Strict 2PL: all exclusive locks are held until commit/abort (shared locks may be released earlier).

4.3 Deadlock detection and prevention

Wait-for edge: Ti → Tj when Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. Deadlock ⇔ cycle.
SchemeOlder requester (TS smaller)Younger requester
Wait-DieWaitsAborts (“dies”)
Wound-WaitWounds — aborts the younger holderWaits

Smaller timestamp = older. Both schemes are deadlock-free because the wait-for graph always points from younger to older.

Worked example (U3-C-14, e1): TS(T1) = 5, TS(T2) = 10, T2 requests a lock held by T1 (younger → older). Wait-Die: T2 aborts. Wound-Wait: T2 waits.

5.Timestamp Ordering & Optimistic Validation

5.1 Basic timestamp ordering (TO)

OperationAbort ifOtherwise
Read(X) by TTS(T) < W-TS(X)Execute; R-TS(X) = max(R-TS(X), TS(T))
Write(X) by TTS(T) < R-TS(X) or TS(T) < W-TS(X)Execute; W-TS(X) = TS(T)

R-TS(X) = largest timestamp of any transaction that read X · W-TS(X) = largest timestamp of any transaction that wrote X. On abort the operations are discarded and timestamps are not restored.

5.2 Thomas Write Rule

Write(X) by T: if TS(T) < R-TS(X) → abort. If R-TS(X) ≤ TS(T) < W-TS(X) → ignore the write. Else execute.
Worked example (U3-C-16, S16a): w2(X) sets W(X) = 2. Then w1(X) with TS = 1: basic TO sees 1 < W = 2 → T1 aborts. Thomas Write Rule: R = 0 ≤ 1 < W = 2 → the write is ignored, T1 continues and both commit. The rule only changes the stale blind-write case.

5.3 Optimistic validation rule

Validation test for Tj against an earlier-validated Ti

Tj passes if finish(Ti) < start(Tj), or both start(Tj) < finish(Ti) < validation(Tj) and WriteSet(Ti) ∩ ReadSet(Tj) = ∅. Any failure ⇒ Tj aborts.

Worked example (U3-C-17, T3 vs T2): finish(T2) = 9, start(T3) = 8, validation(T3) = 10, so 8 < 9 < 10 (overlap). WS(T2) = {C} ∩ RS(T3) = {A,C} = {C} ≠ ∅ → T3 aborts.

6.Recovery Rules

6.1 Log record formats

RecordUsed by
<T,X,new>Deferred modification (new value only)
<T,X,old,new>Immediate modification (both values)
<T,X,old>UNDO-only logging

6.2 Recovery procedure by strategy

StrategyPassesDirectionWhich transactions
DeferredREDO onlyForward, log orderCommitted
ImmediateUNDO then REDOUNDO backward, REDO forwardUNDO: no commit/abort · REDO: committed
UNDO-onlyUNDO onlyBackwardNo commit record

6.3 Checkpoint rules

  • A transaction that committed before the checkpoint → IGNORE (already on disk).
  • A transaction in the checkpoint list that commits after it → REDO from its first write.
  • A transaction with an abort record → IGNORE (already rolled back).
  • Scan start = the earliest start record of any transaction active at the checkpoint.

6.4 Shadow paging rules

  • A modified page is copied to the lowest-numbered free location; the current page table is updated.
  • A page modified twice is copied once (the second write is in place).
  • Commit = make the current table the shadow table, then free the replaced locations.
  • Crash before commit = use the shadow table and reclaim all locations allocated by the failed transaction.
Worked example (U3-D-17): shadow table P1→L3, P2→L7, P3→L1, P4→L5, P5→L2; free L4, L6, L8, L9. T modifies P2 then P5 then P2. Current table after T's writes: P1→L3, P2→L4, P3→L1, P4→L5, P5→L6. Crash before commit → database uses the shadow table (P2→L7, P5→L2); L4 and L6 are reclaimed, free list = L4, L6, L8, L9.

Part 3 — Important Questions & Solutions

A representative selection from the 86-question bank. Every entry keeps its original ID (U3-A-01, U3-B-03, …) so you can locate it in the source. Difficulty (L1–L5) and platform tags are as in the original: Executable runs in a real session, MySQL / Oracle mark platform-specific behaviour, and Manual means a paper exercise — no engine exposes these algorithms.

A.Query Processing & Optimization

Statistics: EMP 50,000 tuples / 1,250 blocks; DEPT 10 tuples / 1 block; WORKS 150,000 tuples / 3,000 blocks; PROJ 200 tuples. Block = 4,000 B.

U3-A-01Query trees, SQL → relational algebra, selection cascadeL1Manual

Problem. For SELECT emp_name FROM u3_emp WHERE dept_id = 3 AND salary > 90000; write the RA expression, draw the canonical tree, and rewrite the selection as a cascade in both orders.

Solution.

RA:      π_emp_name( σ_(dept_id=3 ∧ salary>90000)(EMP) )
Cascade 1: π_emp_name( σ_dept_id=3( σ_salary>90000(EMP) ) )
Cascade 2: π_emp_name( σ_salary>90000( σ_dept_id=3(EMP) ) )

Canonical tree — one conjunctive selection above the leaf:

      π emp_name
          |
   σ dept_id=3 ∧ salary>90000
          |
         EMP

Both cascades are equivalent to the conjunctive selection (rule: σc1∧c2 ≡ σc1 ∘ σc2, and the two single-condition selections commute). In each cascade tree the two σ nodes are simply stacked in the order listed.

U3-A-02EXPLAIN before and after an indexL1Executable

Problem. Inspect the plan for SELECT emp_name FROM u3_emp WHERE salary > 99000; before and after creating an index on salary.

-- MySQL
EXPLAIN SELECT emp_name FROM u3_emp WHERE salary > 99000;
CREATE INDEX idx_sal ON u3_emp(salary);
ANALYZE TABLE u3_emp;
EXPLAIN SELECT emp_name FROM u3_emp WHERE salary > 99000;

-- Oracle
EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT emp_name FROM u3_emp WHERE salary > 99000;
SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY);
CREATE INDEX idx_sal ON u3_emp(salary);
EXEC DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS(USER,'U3_EMP');
EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT emp_name FROM u3_emp WHERE salary > 99000;
SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY);
RunMySQLOracle
Beforetype = ALL, rows ≈ 50,000, Using whereTABLE ACCESS FULL
Aftertype = range, key = idx_sal, rows ≈ 600–650INDEX RANGE SCAN IDX_SAL + TABLE ACCESS BY INDEX ROWID
Expected. Full scan → index range scan, with a large drop in estimated rows.

Related (U3-A-06, FK index behaviour). For the two-table join on dept_id: MySQL already has the FK index fk_emp_dept, so u3_dept usually drives and u3_emp is accessed by ref; with IGNORE INDEX (fk_emp_dept) it falls to a full scan with a join buffer (hash join in 8.0.18+). Oracle has no FK index by default, so creating idx_emp_dept and gathering stats is the comparable step — but Pune is 20 % of the data, so a hash join with full scans may still win. The optimizer is cost-based, so record what you see.

The ≈ 1.25 % figure follows from (99999 − 99000) / 80000. Exact estimates vary with sampled statistics.
U3-A-03Selection pushdown and intermediate sizesL2Manual

Problem. SELECT e.emp_name, d.dept_name FROM u3_emp e, u3_dept d WHERE e.dept_id=d.dept_id AND d.city='Pune' AND e.salary>50000; 2 of 10 departments are in Pune; selectivity of salary>50000 is 0.6. Compute the tuples at every node in the initial and the optimized tree, then the reduction.

Initial tree (Cartesian product first)Tuples
EMP × DEPT50,000 × 10 = 500,000
after all selections50,000 × 0.2 × 0.6 = 6,000
Optimized tree (selection pushed down)Tuples
σsalary>50000(EMP)50,000 × 0.6 = 30,000
σcity='Pune'(DEPT)2
Join30,000 × (2/10) = 6,000
Expected. Initial intermediates ≈ 500,000 (+6,000); optimized 30,000 + 2 + 6,000 = 36,002. Comparing the product with the two selected inputs: 500,000 / 30,002 ≈ 16.7× reduction.

Related (U3-A-16 — classifying conditions). For SELECT e.emp_name FROM EMP e, WORKS w WHERE e.emp_id=w.emp_id AND e.salary>50000 AND e.dept_id=3 AND w.hours>100 AND w.hours*400 > e.salary: e.salary>50000 and e.dept_id=3 are single-relation (EMP), w.hours>100 is single-relation (WORKS), e.emp_id=w.emp_id is the join condition, and w.hours*400 > e.salary is mixed — it cannot be pushed below the join and is applied immediately after it. Optimized sizes: σ_EMP = 50,000 × 0.6 × 0.1 = 3,000; σ_WORKS = 150,000 × 0.2 = 30,000; join = 30,000 × (3,000/50,000) = 1,800; after the mixed condition = 900. The initial tree must first form a 7.5-billion-tuple product. Leaves kept — EMP: emp_id, emp_name, salary; WORKS: emp_id, hours.

U3-A-04Projection pushdown and block estimatesL2Manual

Problem. For πemp_name( EMP ⋈ σcity='Pune'(DEPT) ): pushing the projection onto EMP produces a temp relation (emp_name, dept_id) of 40 B/tuple; the final result tuple is 30 B; the join result is 10,000 tuples. Compute the blocks of EMP, the temp relation and the output.

EMP            : bf = ⌊4000/100⌋ = 40   → 50,000 / 40  = 1,250 blocks
Projected temp : bf = ⌊4000/40⌋  = 100  → 50,000 / 100 =   500 blocks
Final output   : bf = ⌊4000/30⌋  = 133  → ⌈10,000/133⌉ =    76 blocks
Expected. The projection cuts the join's EMP input from 1,250 to 500 blocks — a saving of 750 blocks (60 %).
U3-A-05Join ordering — comparing three plansL3Manual

Problem. EMP ⋈ WORKS ⋈ σloc='Delhi'(PROJ), with 20 of 200 projects in Delhi. Compute each plan's intermediate sizes and rank them.

PlanFirst intermediateSecondSum
A: (EMP ⋈ WORKS) ⋈ σPROJ150,000150,000 × (20/200) = 15,000165,000
B: (σPROJ ⋈ WORKS) ⋈ EMP20 × 750 = 15,00015,00030,000
C: (EMP × σPROJ) ⋈ WORKS50,000 × 20 = 1,000,00015,0001,015,000
Ranking: B < A < C. Plan B applies the selective filter first, so every join runs on a small input. Plan C forms a Cartesian product and is worst.

Related (U3-A-11 — three-way query). For SELECT p.pname FROM PROJ p, WORKS w, EMP e WHERE p.proj_id=w.proj_id AND w.emp_id=e.emp_id AND e.dept_id=3 AND p.loc='Delhi' (dept_id=3 keeps 1/10 of EMP; 20 of 200 projects are in Delhi), the optimized tree is π_pname( (π(σ_loc='Delhi'(PROJ)) ⋈_proj_id π(WORKS)) ⋈_emp_id π(σ_dept_id=3(EMP)) ). Projection lists — PROJ: proj_id, pname · WORKS: emp_id, proj_id · EMP: emp_id. Intermediate sums: (σPROJ ⋈ WORKS) ⋈ σEMP = 15,000 + 1,500 = 16,500; (σEMP ⋈ WORKS) ⋈ σPROJ = 16,500 (a tie); the Cartesian-first plan = 100,000 + 1,500 = 101,500, about 6× worse.

U3-A-07Cost-based optimization — BNL vs index nested loopL3Manual

Problem. Cost EMP ⋈ WORKS on emp_id with M = 52 buffer pages. BNL cost = bouter + ⌈bouter/(M−2)⌉ × binner. A secondary B+ tree on WORKS.emp_id has height 3; each EMP tuple matches 3 WORKS tuples at 1 block I/O per matching tuple. Compare BNL (EMP outer), BNL (WORKS outer) and index nested loop (EMP outer).

(i)  EMP outer   : 1,250 + ⌈1250/50⌉ × 3,000 = 1,250 + 25 × 3,000 =  76,250
(ii) WORKS outer : 3,000 + ⌈3000/50⌉ × 1,250 = 3,000 + 60 × 1,250 =  78,000
(iii) Index NL   : 1,250 + 50,000 × (3 + 3)                       = 301,250
Best is (i) — BNL with EMP as the outer relation. Index nested loop loses because every EMP tuple triggers a probe and the matches are unclustered.

Related: U3-A-12 uses the same BNL formula (M = 12) to compare pushdown with a temp relation (best: 40,500) against no pushdown (376,250) — a ≈ 9.3× ratio.

U3-A-08Access-path selection and break-even pointL4Manual

Problem. SELECT * FROM EMP WHERE dept_id = 3; returns 5,000 tuples. Three candidate paths: linear scan; secondary (unclustered) B+ tree of height 3 at 1 I/O per record; clustered B+ tree of height 3 with contiguous records. Rank them and find the break-even record count.

Linear scan      : 1,250
Secondary index  : 3 + 5,000          = 5,003
Clustered index  : 3 + ⌈5000/40⌉ = 128
Ranking: clustered (128) < scan (1,250) < secondary (5,003). Break-even: 3 + r = 1,250 → r = 1,247 records. Above that, the linear scan beats the secondary index.
U3-A-09Composite index design — column order mattersL4Executable

Problem. For SELECT COUNT(*) FROM u3_emp WHERE dept_id=3 AND salary BETWEEN 90000 AND 99999; create idx_ds(dept_id, salary) and idx_sd(salary, dept_id), force each in turn, and name the better index.

-- MySQL (Oracle uses /*+ INDEX(e idx_ds) */ hints)
EXPLAIN SELECT COUNT(*) FROM u3_emp USE INDEX (idx_ds) WHERE dept_id=3 AND salary BETWEEN 90000 AND 99999;
EXPLAIN SELECT COUNT(*) FROM u3_emp USE INDEX (idx_sd) WHERE dept_id=3 AND salary BETWEEN 90000 AND 99999;
Verdict: idx_ds.

Related (U3-A-13, subquery vs join). WHERE dept_id IN (SELECT dept_id FROM u3_dept WHERE city='Delhi') and the equivalent join are usually rewritten to the same semijoin by a modern optimizer (MySQL and Oracle both unnest the IN subquery), so the plans are often identical. Delhi holds 3 of 10 departments, so a hash join or a join-buffered scan on EMP is plausible. This is version- and statistics-dependent — record what you observe rather than assuming.

 Equality on the leading column plus a range on the second narrows the index range directly (estimated rows ≈ 5,000 × 12.5 % ≈ 600). idx_sd scans the whole salary range (≈ 6,000 entries) and filters dept_id inside the index — about 10× more entries touched. Both are covering for COUNT(*). Estimates are statistics-dependent.

Related (U3-A-14): with idx_ds forced, SELECT dept_id, salary … is answered from the index alone (MySQL Using index; Oracle shows only the INDEX RANGE SCAN), while SELECT emp_name … needs table row lookups (Oracle adds TABLE ACCESS BY INDEX ROWID).

U3-A-10Query rewriting and sargability (real-world slow report)L5Executable

Problem. An HR report on March-2016 hires is slow. Index hire_date, then compare the original function-wrapped predicate with a half-open range rewrite.

-- original (not sargable: the column is wrapped in a function)
MySQL : WHERE DATE_FORMAT(hire_date,'%Y-%m') = '2016-03'
Oracle: WHERE TO_CHAR(hire_date,'YYYY-MM')   = '2016-03'
-- rewrite (sargable: half-open date range)
MySQL : WHERE hire_date >= '2016-03-01' AND hire_date < '2016-04-01'
Oracle: WHERE hire_date >= DATE '2016-03-01' AND hire_date < DATE '2016-04-01'
Original: full scan (or full index scan), ≈ 50,000 estimated rows — the index cannot be range-seeked. Rewrite: MySQL type = range, key = idx_hire, ≈ 500 rows; Oracle INDEX RANGE SCAN IDX_HIRE. The ≈ 1.03 % follows from 31 of 3,000 days.
U3-A-11Three-way query: heuristic steps, projection lists, sizesL3Manual

Problem. SELECT p.pname FROM PROJ p, WORKS w, EMP e WHERE p.proj_id=w.proj_id AND w.emp_id=e.emp_id AND e.dept_id=3 AND p.loc='Delhi'; dept_id=3 selects 1/10 of EMP; 20 of 200 projects are in Delhi. Apply the heuristics and compute intermediate sizes.

Optimized tree:
π_pname( ( π_(proj_id,pname)(σ_loc='Delhi'(PROJ)) ⋈_proj_id π_(emp_id,proj_id)(WORKS) )
            ⋈_emp_id π_emp_id(σ_dept_id=3(EMP)) )

Projection lists — PROJ: proj_id, pname · WORKS: emp_id, proj_id · EMP: emp_id
PlanFirst intermediateSecondSum
(σPROJ ⋈ WORKS) ⋈ σEMP20 × 750 = 15,00015,000 × 0.1 = 1,50016,500
(σEMP ⋈ WORKS) ⋈ σPROJ5,000 × 3 = 15,00015,000 × (20/200) = 1,50016,500
σEMP × σPROJ, then ⋈ WORKS5,000 × 20 = 100,0001,500101,500
Expected. The first two join orders tie; the Cartesian-first plan is ≈ 6× worse and should be avoided. Heuristic steps in order: split the selection, push dept_id=3 to EMP and loc='Delhi' to PROJ, turn the two equalities into joins, run the most selective join first, push projections.
U3-A-15Index effect on ORDER BY / top-N queriesL2Executable

Problem. Run EXPLAIN for the top-10 salaries, create idx_sal(salary), and repeat.

EXPLAIN SELECT emp_id, salary FROM u3_emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 10;   -- MySQL
CREATE INDEX idx_sal ON u3_emp(salary);
EXPLAIN SELECT emp_id, salary FROM u3_emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 10;

-- Oracle (12c+): WHERE salary IS NOT NULL is required, see below
EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT emp_id, salary FROM u3_emp WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
                 ORDER BY salary DESC FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY;
RunMySQLOracle
Beforetype = ALL, Extra: Using filesort, rows ≈ 50,000TABLE ACCESS FULL + SORT ORDER BY STOPKEY
Aftertype = index, key = idx_sal, Extra: Backward index scantypically INDEX FULL SCAN DESCENDING IDX_SAL + COUNT STOPKEY (no sort)
Why Oracle needs IS NOT NULL

Oracle B-tree indexes do not store rows whose indexed key is entirely NULL. salary is nullable, so without the predicate Oracle cannot use the index to return all rows in order. MySQL has no such restriction. Oracle's choice is still cost-based — confirm it in your output.

B.Transaction Processing

All Section B questions are executable. Run the reset script (UPDATE u3_account …; COMMIT;) before each exercise. Starting balances: 101 = 10000, 102 = 5000, 103 = 20000, 104 = 800.

U3-B-01COMMIT — a multi-row transferL1Executable

Task. Transfer 2,000 from 101 to 102 in one transaction and commit; display all balances.

START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance = balance - 2000 WHERE acc_no = 101;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance = balance + 2000 WHERE acc_no = 102;
COMMIT;
SELECT * FROM u3_account;
Expected: 101 = 8000, 102 = 7000, 103 = 20000, 104 = 800. Oracle: identical, minus START TRANSACTION (a transaction begins at the first DML; optionally SET TRANSACTION READ WRITE; first).
U3-B-02ROLLBACK — atomicityL1Executable

Task. Debit 3,000 from 101, SELECT, ROLLBACK, SELECT again.

START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance = balance - 3000 WHERE acc_no = 101;
SELECT balance FROM u3_account WHERE acc_no = 101;   -- 7000 inside the transaction
ROLLBACK;
SELECT balance FROM u3_account WHERE acc_no = 101;   -- 10000 after rollback
Oracle note

Same without START TRANSACTION. If a worksheet auto-commits each statement, run the whole sequence as one script or PL/SQL block, otherwise the ROLLBACK has nothing to undo.

U3-B-03SAVEPOINT and partial rollback (with a consistency flaw to spot)L2Executable

Task. In one transaction: debit 101 by 1,000 → SAVEPOINT s1 → credit 102 by 1,000 → SAVEPOINT s2 → debit 103 by 5,000 → ROLLBACK TO s2 → credit 104 by 500 → COMMIT. Then compare the total of all balances.

START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance=balance-1000 WHERE acc_no=101;
SAVEPOINT s1;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance=balance+1000 WHERE acc_no=102;
SAVEPOINT s2;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance=balance-5000 WHERE acc_no=103;
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s2;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance=balance+500  WHERE acc_no=104;
COMMIT;
SELECT *, (SELECT SUM(balance) FROM u3_account) AS total FROM u3_account;
Expected: 101 = 9000, 102 = 6000, 103 = 20000, 104 = 1300. Total 36,300 against 35,800 initially. Flaw: the 500 credit to 104 has no matching debit, so the transaction violates conservation of money. Rolling back to s2 undid only the 103 debit.

Related (U3-B-09, SAVEPOINT name reuse): debit 101 by 1,000 → SAVEPOINT a → credit 102 by 500 → SAVEPOINT a again → credit 103 by 500 → ROLLBACK TO a → COMMIT. Final: 101 = 9000, 102 = 5500, 103 = 20000, 104 = 800. Re-issuing SAVEPOINT a replaces the earlier savepoint of that name in both databases, so only the 103 credit was undone.

U3-B-04ACID — atomicity and consistency through a constraint failureL2Executable

Task. Transfer 1,000 from 104 (balance 800) to 101 by crediting 101 first, then debiting 104. Record the error, inspect the intermediate state, then ROLLBACK.

START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance=balance+1000 WHERE acc_no=101;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance=balance-1000 WHERE acc_no=104;   -- fails (balance would be -200)
SELECT acc_no,balance FROM u3_account WHERE acc_no IN (101,104);
ROLLBACK;
SELECT acc_no,balance FROM u3_account WHERE acc_no IN (101,104);
Stage101104Note
Intermediate11000800Credit still pending; only the failed statement is undone, not the transaction
After ROLLBACK10000800Atomicity restored
Error text

MySQL: ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'chk_bal' is violated.
Oracle: ORA-02290: check constraint (…CHK_BAL) violated

Related (U3-B-11, bulk update and rollback). Record SUM(salary) for dept_id = 4, then in one transaction give the department a 10 % raise: ROW_COUNT() reports 5,000 rows, and the sum inside the transaction is exactly 1.10 × the original (salaries are whole numbers, so ×1.10 gives exact two-decimal values). After ROLLBACK the sum is back to the original — atomicity across many rows. Oracle reports “5000 rows updated”, or use SQL%ROWCOUNT in a block.

U3-B-05Isolation — two sessions, two isolation levelsL3Executable

Task. Run the timeline below in two sessions, once per isolation level, and record what A sees at steps 1 and 3.

StepSession ASession B
1Start a transaction; SELECT balance for 101—
2—Debit 101 by 2,000; COMMIT
3SELECT balance for 101 again—
ModeA at step 1A at step 3Why
MySQL REPEATABLE READ (default)1000010000Consistent snapshot from the transaction's first read
MySQL READ COMMITTED100008000Each statement sees the latest committed data
Oracle READ COMMITTED (default)100008000Same as MySQL READ COMMITTED
Oracle SERIALIZABLE1000010000Snapshot isolation; a later UPDATE fails with ORA-08177

Extension. In the serializable run, letting A attempt UPDATE … WHERE acc_no=101 after step 3 fails with ORA-08177: can't serialize access for this transaction.

U3-B-06Lost update and row lockingL3Executable

Part 1 — no locks. Both sessions read 101's balance (10000). A writes 9000 and commits; B writes 10500 and commits.

Final 10500 — A's debit is lost, because B overwrote it from a stale read.

Part 2 — with SELECT … FOR UPDATE.

-- A START TRANSACTION; SELECT balance FROM u3_account WHERE acc_no=101 FOR UPDATE;  -- 10000
-- B START TRANSACTION; SELECT balance FROM u3_account WHERE acc_no=101 FOR UPDATE;  -- B BLOCKS
-- A UPDATE u3_account SET balance=balance-1000 WHERE acc_no=101; COMMIT;
-- B -- unblocks, reads 9000
       UPDATE u3_account SET balance=balance+500 WHERE acc_no=101; COMMIT;
Final 9500. B waited for A's exclusive lock. In MySQL, B errors with 1205 if A holds the lock past innodb_lock_wait_timeout (default 50 s). Oracle uses the same syntax and B also waits.
U3-B-07Multi-table transaction with conditional stock deductionL4Executable

Task. Use conditional updates (… AND stock >= qty) and check the affected-row count. Txn 1 orders Laptop ×3 and Mouse ×10; Txn 2 orders Mouse ×5 then Laptop ×3, and rolls back the whole transaction if any line affects 0 rows. Stock starts Laptop = 5, Mouse = 50.

START TRANSACTION;                                    -- Txn 1
UPDATE u3_product SET stock=stock-3  WHERE prod_id=1 AND stock>=3;   -- 1 row
INSERT INTO u3_orders(prod_id,qty) VALUES (1,3);
UPDATE u3_product SET stock=stock-10 WHERE prod_id=2 AND stock>=10;  -- 1 row
INSERT INTO u3_orders(prod_id,qty) VALUES (2,10);
COMMIT;

START TRANSACTION;                                    -- Txn 2
UPDATE u3_product SET stock=stock-5 WHERE prod_id=2 AND stock>=5;    -- 1 row
UPDATE u3_product SET stock=stock-3 WHERE prod_id=1 AND stock>=3;    -- 0 rows (stock = 2)
ROLLBACK;
Expected. After Txn 1: Laptop = 2, Mouse = 40, 2 order rows. After Txn 2: unchanged — the Mouse deduction and its order row were undone together with the failed Laptop line.

Oracle (Txn 2 as PL/SQL): check SQL%ROWCOUNT = 0 after each update and ROLLBACK; RETURN; — same outcome.

U3-B-08Concurrent seat booking — SKIP LOCKED vs NOWAITL5Executable

Problem. Two agents book the first available seat on train 12001 at the same moment. Neither may get the other's seat.

-- MySQL, session A
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT seat_no FROM u3_seat WHERE train_no=12001 AND status='FREE'
  ORDER BY seat_no LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;      -- 1
UPDATE u3_seat SET status='BOOKED', passenger='Asha' WHERE train_no=12001 AND seat_no=1;

-- MySQL, session B (before A commits) — skips the locked seat
SELECT seat_no FROM u3_seat WHERE train_no=12001 AND status='FREE'
  ORDER BY seat_no LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;      -- 2
UPDATE u3_seat SET status='BOOKED', passenger='Ravi' WHERE train_no=12001 AND seat_no=2;
Expected. seat 1 = Asha, seat 2 = Ravi, seats 3–6 FREE. Without SKIP LOCKED, B's SELECT … FOR UPDATE waits on A's lock on seat 1 until A commits or the 1205 timeout fires.
Why Oracle is different

Oracle does not allow a row-limiting clause together with FOR UPDATE, so there is no direct equivalent of ORDER BY … LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. The unit uses a per-seat FOR UPDATE NOWAIT loop instead: A locks seat 1; B's attempt on seat 1 raises ORA-00054: resource busy and acquire with NOWAIT specified, so B falls back to seat 2. A cursor-based FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED would lock every free seat when opened, leaving B nothing.

Related (U3-B-12, three-statement atomic transaction). Txn X: Mouse ×4 (price 500) — insert order, decrement stock guarded by stock >= 4, debit 101 by 2,000; commit → Mouse = 46, 1 order row, account 101 = 8,000. Txn Y: Laptop ×1 (price 55,000) — the debit fails with ERROR 3819, so ROLLBACK leaves everything unchanged. The next order_id skips the value consumed by Y's rolled-back insert: AUTO_INCREMENT / identity values are not rolled back, which is not an atomicity failure.

U3-B-10When a transaction really starts — autocommitL2Executable

Task. Test the effect of autocommit on ROLLBACK.

SET autocommit = 1;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE acc_no = 101;
ROLLBACK;
SELECT balance FROM u3_account WHERE acc_no = 101;    -- 9000 (already committed)

SET autocommit = 0;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE acc_no = 101;
ROLLBACK;
SELECT balance FROM u3_account WHERE acc_no = 101;    -- 9000

SET autocommit = 1;
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE acc_no = 101;
ROLLBACK;
SELECT balance FROM u3_account WHERE acc_no = 101;    -- 10000 (rollback worked)
Expected. With autocommit = 1 a lone ROLLBACK does nothing. START TRANSACTION suspends autocommit for that one transaction, so the rollback works. Oracle: SET AUTOCOMMIT ON/OFF — a client feature, not a database one; a browser worksheet's behaviour depends on the tool, so record what yours does.

C.Concurrency Control

Notation: r1(A) T1 reads A · w1(A) T1 writes A · c1 T1 commits · a1 T1 aborts. Schedules read left to right. Neither MySQL nor Oracle lets you configure timestamp ordering, optimistic validation or a precedence-graph checker, so those questions are Manual; I have invented no commands for them.

U3-C-02Precedence graphs and conflict serializabilityL1Manual

Schedules. S2a: r1(A) w1(A) r2(A) w2(A) r1(B) w1(B) r2(B) w2(B). S2b: r1(A) r2(A) w2(A) w1(A).

S2a. On A, w1(A) precedes r2(A) and w2(A) → T1→T2; same on B → T1→T2. The graph is acyclic, so S2a is conflict serializable, equivalent to serial order T1, T2.
S2b. r1(A) before w2(A) → T1→T2; r2(A) before w1(A) → T2→T1. The cycle makes S2b not conflict serializable.

Related (U3-C-03, conflict equivalence). For S3 = w1(A) r2(A) w1(B) r3(B) w2(C) w3(D) the edges are T1→T2 (A) and T1→T3 (B), with T2 and T3 unordered — the serial orders are T1,T2,T3 and T1,T3,T2. For Sx = r1(A) w1(A) r2(A) r1(B) w2(B), the schedule Sy = r1(A) w1(A) r1(B) r2(A) w2(B) keeps both conflicting pairs in the same order, so it is conflict equivalent; Sz = r1(A) r2(A) w2(B) w1(A) r1(B) reverses both pairs (r2(A) before w1(A), w2(B) before r1(B)) and is therefore not equivalent — it matches serial T2,T1 instead.

Related (U3-C-24): for S24 = w1(A) r2(A) w3(B) r4(B) w2(C) r4(C) r1(D) w3(D) the acyclic graph gives serial orders T1,T2,T3,T4 and T1,T3,T2,T4. Appending w2(D) adds T3→T2 and leaves the unique order T1,T3,T2,T4.

U3-C-04Cycle detection and transaction removal (tricky)L4Manual

Schedule S4. r1(X) w2(X) r3(Y) w1(Y) r4(Z) w3(Z) w4(X). Draw the graph, list every simple cycle, and test whether deleting each single transaction makes the rest serializable.

Edges : X → T1→T2, T1→T4, T2→T4
        Y → T3→T1
        Z → T4→T3
Cycles: T1→T4→T3→T1   and   T1→T2→T4→T3→T1
DeleteRemaining edgesSerializable?
T1T2→T4, T4→T3Yes
T2T1→T4, T4→T3, T3→T1 — cycle survivesNo
T3T1→T2, T1→T4, T2→T4Yes
T4T1→T2, T3→T1Yes
U3-C-05View serializability — blind writesL3Manual

Schedules. S5a: r1(A) w2(A) w1(A) w3(A). S5b: w1(A) w2(A) w2(B) w1(B) w3(A) w3(B).

S5a. Conflict test: r1(A) before w2(A) → T1→T2; w2(A) before w1(A) → T2→T1. Cycle → not conflict serializable. View test: r1 reads the initial value (T1 first) and T3 makes the final write (T3 last). Only T1, T2, T3 satisfies both → view serializable.

S5b. Cycle on A → not conflict serializable. There are no reads, and the final writes of A and B are both by T3, so any order with T3 last matches → view serializable as T1,T2,T3 or T2,T1,T3.

Pattern to remember

A schedule that is view serializable but not conflict serializable always owes it to a blind write whose value is overwritten before any read. U3-C-06 gives the negative cases: S6 (r1(A) r2(A) w1(A) w2(A)) and S7 (r1(A) w2(A) r3(A) w1(A)) are neither conflict nor view serializable, because the required order constraints contradict each other. U3-C-25 applies the same reasoning to S25a (not view serializable) and S25b (view serializable only as T1,T2,T3).

Related (U3-C-01, conflicting operations): for S1 = r1(A) w2(A) r2(B) w1(B) r3(A) w3(B) the conflicting pairs are (r1(A),w2(A)), (w2(A),r3(A)), (r2(B),w1(B)), (r2(B),w3(B)) and (w1(B),w3(B)) — 5 pairs. The pair (r1(A),r3(A)) is read/read, so it does not conflict.

U3-C-07Recoverable, cascadeless and strict — the 7-schedule tableL2Manual
ScheduleRecoverableCascadelessStrictReason
R1: w1(A) r2(A) c1 c2YesNoNoT2 reads from T1 before c1, but c1 precedes c2
R2: w1(A) r2(A) c2 c1NoNoNoT2 reads from T1 and commits before c1
R3: w1(A) c1 r2(A) w2(A) c2YesYesYesReads/writes occur only after c1
R4: w1(A) w2(A) c1 c2YesYesNoNo reads, but T2 overwrites uncommitted w1(A)
R5: w1(A) r2(A) w2(B) a1 c2NoNoNoT2 read from T1, T1 aborted, T2 committed
R6: w1(A) r2(A) a1 a2YesNoNoT2 read from T1 before a1 (cascade abort)
R7: w1(A) w2(A) a1 c2YesYesNoT2 overwrote uncommitted w1(A); a1's before-image restore would destroy T2's write
Read the pattern, not the rows. Not recoverable ⇔ a read-from pair commits out of order. Not cascadeless ⇔ some read is of an uncommitted value. Not strict ⇔ someone touches an item whose last writer is still uncommitted (the “overwrite” rows R4, R7 have no reads at all).

Related (U3-C-09, cascading rollback). For S9 = w1(A) r2(A) w2(B) r3(B) w3(C) r4(C) w5(D) r6(D) a1 with nothing yet committed: the abort set is T1 (explicit), T2 (read A from T1), T3 (read B from T2) and T4 (read C from T3); T5 and T6 survive (T5 read nothing dirty, T6 read D from T5). If c2 had occurred just before a1, T2 would have committed after reading T1's dirty A while T1 never commits — not recoverable, violating pair (T2 reads from T1 and commits while T1 aborts).

U3-C-10Shared and exclusive locks — real lock compatibilityL3Executable

Task (MySQL). A holds FOR SHARE on 101; B takes FOR SHARE (granted at once — S/S compatible). Inspect performance_schema.data_locks, then have B attempt an UPDATE and re-inspect.

SELECT ENGINE_TRANSACTION_ID, OBJECT_NAME, INDEX_NAME, LOCK_TYPE, LOCK_MODE, LOCK_STATUS, LOCK_DATA
FROM performance_schema.data_locks;
Observed. Both transactions hold table-level IS locks plus record-level S,REC_NOT_GAP locks with LOCK_STATUS = GRANTED. After B's update, an extra X,REC_NOT_GAP row for B shows LOCK_STATUS = WAITING. A plain SELECT is a consistent non-locking read and returns immediately. If A had issued an UPDATE instead of committing, the two X-lock upgrades deadlock (error 1213).
Oracle

Oracle row reads take no locks and there is no shared row lock, so the unit uses table locks: LOCK TABLE u3_account IN SHARE MODE; is granted to both sessions, but an UPDATE then waits for A. A lock view (v$lock) needs privileges. If both sessions hold SHARE locks and both try to update, one gets ORA-00060.

Related (U3-C-30, lock waits and timeouts). With A holding a lock on 101: MySQL SET SESSION innodb_lock_wait_timeout = 3; then an UPDATE gives ERROR 1205 after ≈ 3 s; FOR UPDATE NOWAIT gives ERROR 3572; FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED returns an empty set. Oracle gives ORA-00054 (NOWAIT), ORA-30006 (WAIT 3) and no rows (SKIP LOCKED). A plain Oracle UPDATE has no default timeout and waits indefinitely. By default (innodb_rollback_on_timeout OFF) a MySQL timeout rolls back only the statement, so B's transaction stays open.

U3-C-11Strict 2PL simulation with a deadlockL3Manual

Transactions. T1 = r(A) w(B) w(A) commit. T2 = r(A) w(B) commit (started after T1). Arrival order: r1(A), r2(A), w1(B), w2(B), w1(A). Strict 2PL; upgrades allowed; on deadlock abort the younger and restart it.

#OperationLock requestResult
1r1(A)S(A) by T1Granted
2r2(A)S(A) by T2Granted (S/S)
3w1(B)X(B) by T1Granted
4w2(B)X(B) by T2Blocked (T1 holds X(B))
5w1(A)upgrade S→X(A) by T1Blocked (T2 holds S(A))
Wait-for graph: T2→T1 and T1→T2 → deadlock. Victim: T2 (younger); it aborts and releases S(A). T1's upgrade is granted, w1(A) runs, T1 commits. T2 restarts: r2(A), w2(B), c2.
Executed schedule: r1(A) r2(A) w1(B) w1(A) c1 r2(A) w2(B) c2 — equivalent to serial T1, T2.

Related (U3-C-26, strict 2PL with lock points). T1 = r(A) w(A) r(B) c, T2 = w(B) r(A) c, arrival r1(A), w2(B), r2(A), w1(A), c2, r1(B), c1. T1's upgrade to X(A) is blocked by T2's S(A); c2 releases it, so the executed schedule is r1(A) w2(B) r2(A) c2 w1(A) r1(B) c1 — equivalent to serial T2, T1. Lock points: T2 = S(A), T1 = S(B). The schedule is recoverable, cascadeless and strict, since T1 touches B only after c2.

U3-C-122PL vs strict 2PL and lock pointsL2Manual

Notation. S(X) shared lock · X(X) exclusive lock · U(X) unlock · c commit.

Te: S(A) r(A) X(B) w(B) U(B) S(C) r(C) c U(A) U(C)No (S(C) after U(B))No–
Rule to apply. 2PL fails the moment a lock is acquired after any lock is released. Strict 2PL additionally fails if an exclusive lock is released before commit — releasing a shared lock early is legal in both.
U3-C-13Deadlock detection, wait-for graph and victim selectionL4Manual

T1X(A)X(B)10
T2X(B)X(C)4
T3X(C)X(A)7

Queue on A is T3 first, then T4; locks are granted in queue order.

Edges: T1→T2, T2→T3, T3→T1, T4→T1, T5→T4. One cycle: T1→T2→T3→T1. Deadlocked: T1, T2, T3. Only blocked: T4 and T5 — they are not on the cycle.
Victim: abort T2 (cost 4), the cheapest on the cycle. Aborting T4 or T5 would leave the deadlock intact.
After T2 aborts: X(B) is released and T1's queued request is granted → T1 finishes. T3 is first in A's queue, so T3 gets X(A) and finishes. Then T4 gets A and finishes, and T5 gets X(D). Completion order: T1, T3, T4, T5; T2 restarts afterwards.
U3-C-14Deadlock prevention — Wait-Die vs Wound-WaitL3Manual

Setup. TS(T1) = 5, TS(T2) = 10, TS(T3) = 15 — smaller means older. Wait-Die: an older requester waits, a younger requester dies. Wound-Wait: an older requester wounds (aborts) the younger holder, a younger requester waits.

Event (requester → holder)Wait-DieWound-Wait
e1: T2→T1 (younger requests)T2 abortsT2 waits
e2: T1→T3 (older requests)T1 waitsT3 aborts
e3: T3→T2 (younger requests)T3 abortsT3 waits
e4: T2→T3 (older requests)T2 waitsT3 aborts
e5: T1→T2 (older requests)T1 waitsT2 aborts

Related (U3-C-27): with T3 holding X(A), T2 holding X(B), T1 holding X(C) and requests T1→A, T2→C, T3→B: Wait-Die aborts T2 and commits in the order T3, T1, T2; Wound-Wait aborts T3 and commits T1, T2, T3.

U3-C-15Timestamp ordering (basic TO)L4Manual

Setup. TS(T1) = 1, TS(T2) = 2, TS(T3) = 3; items A, B, C start with R-TS = W-TS = 0. Schedule S15: r2(A) w3(A) r1(A) w1(B) r3(B) w2(B) c3. Aborted operations are discarded and timestamps are not restored.

StepOpCheckOutcomeA (R,W)B (R,W)
0init––(0,0)(0,0)
1r2(A)2 ≥ W = 0OK(2,0)(0,0)
2w3(A)3 ≥ R = 2, ≥ W = 0OK(2,3)(0,0)
3r1(A)1 < W = 3T1 aborts(2,3)(0,0)
4w1(B)T1 aborteddiscarded(2,3)(0,0)

Aborts: T1 and T2. Only T3 commits, and nothing T3 read was written by an aborted transaction, so there is no cascade.
Restarts. T1′ (TS 4): r(A) → A (4,3); w(B) → B (3,4). T2′ (TS 5): r(A) → A (5,3); w(B) → B (3,5). Final: A (R=5, W=3), B (R=3, W=5).

Related (U3-C-28) runs a larger schedule under basic TO and under the Thomas Write Rule: basic TO aborts T1 and T2 with final X(10,30) Y(20,0) Z(30,20); with Thomas, only T1 aborts and T2 continues.

U3-C-16Thomas Write Rule — where it differs from basic TOL4Manual

Setup. TS(T1) = 1, TS(T2) = 2; X and Y start at 0.

S16a: w2(X) w1(X) r1(Y) w1(Y)w2(X) sets W(X)=2. w1(X): 1 < W=2 → T1 aborts; only T2 commitsw1(X) is ignored (R=0 ≤ 1 < W=2). r1(Y), w1(Y) run → both commit. X (0,2), Y (1,1)
S16b: r2(X) w1(X) r1(Y) w1(Y)r2(X) sets R(X)=2. w1(X): 1 < R=2 → T1 abortsSame — 1 < R-TS → T1 aborts
S16c: w2(X) r1(X) w1(Y)r1(X): 1 < W=2 → T1 abortsSame — the read rule is unchanged
Key point. The rule changes only the stale blind write case (S16a), which is not a read conflict. For S16a the result is equivalent to serial T1, T2, because T2's write to X overwrites T1's ignored write.

Rule. Tj passes against every earlier-validated, non-aborted Ti if either finish(Ti) < start(Tj), or start(Tj) < finish(Ti) < validation(Tj) and WriteSet(Ti) ∩ ReadSet(Tj) = ∅.

Related (U3-C-29): a five-transaction variant. T2 aborts (WS(T1)={B} ∩ RS(T2)={B}) and T5 aborts (WS(T3)={D} ∩ RS(T5)={B,D}={D}); T1, T3 and T4 commit. Restarting T2 and T5 at start 14 / validation 15 lets both commit, since all earlier finishers are before 14.

U3-C-19Real deadlock — DBMS detection (MySQL vs Oracle)L4Executable

Timeline. A debits 101; B debits 102; A debits 102 (blocks); B debits 101 → deadlock.

-- MySQL error in one session:
ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G          -- LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK section

-- Oracle error after about 3 s:
ORA-00060: deadlock detected while waiting for resource
Corrected solution (the source flags an earlier wording error here).
MySQL (InnoDB): the detector rolls back the entire transaction of the victim; the other session's blocked statement then completes and commits. Both transactions debit 101 and 102 by 100 each, so the committed result is the same whichever session is chosen: 101 = 9900, 102 = 4900.
Oracle: ORA-00060 rolls back only the statement that raised it. That session keeps its earlier update and its lock, so the other session stays blocked until the first ends its transaction. If the erroring session then issues ROLLBACK: 101 = 9900, 102 = 4900. If it issues COMMIT instead: 102 was debited twice and 101 once → 101 = 9900, 102 = 4800.

Prevention. Both sessions update 101 then 102 (ascending account number). The second session simply waits at its first statement and no cycle forms.

U3-C-20Isolation anomalies — dirty read and phantomL3Executable

Part 1 — dirty read. A debits 101 by 3,000 without committing; B reads 101.

B's isolation levelB seesNote
MySQL READ UNCOMMITTED7000Dirty read; after A's ROLLBACK, B reads 10000
MySQL READ COMMITTED10000No dirty read
Oracle (any level)10000Oracle has no READ UNCOMMITTED

Part 2 — phantom. A counts employees with dept_id = 3; B inserts a new row and commits; A counts again.

A's modeSecond countNote
MySQL REPEATABLE READ (default)5000Snapshot; the phantom appears only on a current read (… FOR SHARE → 5001)
Oracle READ COMMITTED5001Phantom visible
Oracle SERIALIZABLE5000Phantom blocked
Part 3 — MySQL gap locking (observe, do not assume)

After the extra row is deleted and committed, A runs SELECT … WHERE dept_id=3 FOR UPDATE. InnoDB takes next-key/gap locks on the fk_emp_dept index range, so B's insert blocks until A commits — or until innodb_lock_wait_timeout (default 50 s) fires with error 1205. This relies on InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ gap locking, so confirm it on your own server.

Related (U3-C-18, optimistic control with an application-level version column — executable). A and B both read balance/version of 101 (10000, 0). A does UPDATE … SET balance = 9000, version = version + 1 WHERE acc_no = 101 AND version = 0 (ROW_COUNT() = 1) and commits. B's same guard on version = 0 returns 0 rows — the conflict is detected. B re-reads (9000, 1), recomputes 9500 with AND version = 1 (1 row) and commits. Final: 9500, version 2 — no update is lost. This is OCC implemented with a version column, not the DBMS's own validation phase.

U3-C-21Serializability and recoverability together (banking)L5Manual

Scenario. X = 101, Y = 102, Z = 103. T1 moves 101→102, T2 moves 102→103, T3 posts interest to 101 and 103. Operations: r1(X) w1(X) r3(X) w3(X) r2(Y) w2(Y) r1(Y) w1(Y) r2(Z) w2(Z) r3(Z) w3(Z); then c1, c2, c3.

Precedence graph. X: T1→T3. Y: T2→T1. Z: T2→T3. Acyclic → conflict serializable, serial order T2, T1, T3.
Reads-from: T3 reads X from T1; T1 reads Y from T2; T3 reads Z from T2.
Recoverable? No — c1, c2, c3 is wrong: T1 read Y from T2 but commits before T2.
Corrected commit order: c2, c1, c3 (satisfies c2<c1 from T1 reading T2, c1<c3 from T3 reading T1, and c2<c3 from T3 reading T2).
Cascadeless? No — r3(X), r1(Y) and r3(Z) all read uncommitted writes, so an abort of T2 would cascade.
U3-C-22Comparing protocols — strict 2PL vs timestamp orderingL4Manual

S22a: r1(A) w2(A) c2 r1(B) c1

ProtocolOutcome
Conflict serializable?Yes — T1→T2, serial order T1, T2
Strict 2PLT1 holds S(A) until c1, so w2(A) blocks. Result: r1(A) r1(B) c1 w2(A) c2 (serial). The original interleaving is not producible
Basic TO, TS(T1)=1, TS(T2)=2r1(A) → R(A)=1; w2(A): 2 ≥ 1 OK → W(A)=2; r1(B) OK. All commit
Basic TO, TS(T1)=2, TS(T2)=1r1(A) → R(A)=2; w2(A): 1 < R=2 → T2 aborts; T1 commits

S22b: r1(A) r2(A) w2(A) w1(A) c1 c2

ProtocolOutcome
Conflict serializable?No — cycle T1→T2→T1
Strict 2PLBoth hold S(A); both upgrades block → deadlock. Victim T2 (younger); T1 completes and T2 restarts
Basic TO, TS(T1)=1, TS(T2)=2R=1, then R=2; w2(A) OK (W=2); w1(A): 1 < R=2 → T1 aborts; T2 commits
Basic TO, TS(T1)=2, TS(T2)=1R=2; r2(A) OK; w2(A): 1 < R=2 → T2 aborts; w1(A) OK → T1 commits
Take-away. A conflict-serializable schedule can be rejected by strict 2PL yet accepted by TO (S22a); a non-serializable schedule is rejected by both, but the mechanism differs (deadlock vs abort).

Related (U3-C-31, lost update on railway seats). S = 10 available seats; T1 and T2 each do r(S) then w(S) = read − 1, schedule r1(S) r2(S) w1(S) w2(S) c1 c2. Plain result: S = 9, but the correct value is 8 — a lost update; not conflict serializable. Under strict 2PL (S at read, upgrade at write) both upgrades block → deadlock, victim T2, final S = 8. With an X lock at read (SELECT … FOR UPDATE): executed r1(S) w1(S) c1 r2(S) w2(S) c2 → S = 8, no deadlock.

U3-C-23Concurrent bookings on a unique constraintL5Executable

Scenario. Reception desks A and B both book DrRao at 2026-11-20 10:00 (unique key on doctor + slot_time).

-- A START TRANSACTION;
    INSERT INTO u3_appt(doctor, slot_time, patient) VALUES ('DrRao','2026-11-20 10:00:00','Asha');
-- B START TRANSACTION;
    INSERT INTO u3_appt(doctor, slot_time, patient) VALUES ('DrRao','2026-11-20 10:00:00','Ravi');  -- BLOCKS
-- A COMMIT;
-- B now fails:
ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry 'DrRao-2026-11-20 10:00:00' for key 'u3_appt.uq_doc_slot'
RunBehaviour
Run 1 (A commits)B waits for A, then gets the duplicate-key error
Run 2 (A rolls back)B's insert succeeds — Ravi holds the 10:00 slot
Run 3 (different slots 10:00 / 10:30)No blocking; both succeed
Expected. After Run 1, B's transaction is still open (a failed statement does not roll back the whole transaction), so B can insert Ravi at 10:30 and commit. Final: Asha 10:00, Ravi 10:30. Oracle: B's identical insert waits, then fails with ORA-00001: unique constraint (SCHEMA.UQ_DOC_SLOT) violated; the same statement-level rollback behaviour applies.

D.Database Recovery

Neither MySQL nor Oracle lets you switch on deferred modification, shadow paging or a manual UNDO/REDO pass. Questions D-01 to D-04 and D-23 are Executable (real transaction failure and rollback); D-05 onwards are Manual paper simulations of the recovery algorithms. Log notation is in Part 1 §D.2. Initial values are given in each question.

D.1 — Executable: transaction failure and rollback

U3-D-01Statement-level UNDO after a constraint failureL2Executable
UPDATE u3_account SET balance = balance - 1000;   -- ERROR 3819: Check constraint 'chk_bal' is violated.
SELECT * FROM u3_account;                          -- 10000, 5000, 20000, 800 (nothing changed)

START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE acc_no = 101;
UPDATE u3_account SET balance = balance - 1000;                 -- fails again
SELECT * FROM u3_account;                          -- 101 = 9900, others unchanged
ROLLBACK;
SELECT * FROM u3_account;                          -- 101 = 10000
Expected. The failed multi-row statement is undone as a unit, including rows changed before 104 failed. The earlier 100 debit survives because only the statement was rolled back, not the transaction — the final ROLLBACK/COMMIT decides its fate. Oracle: same statements, error ORA-02290: check constraint (…CHK_BAL) violated.
U3-D-02Limits of ROLLBACK — implicit commit by DDLL2Executable
START TRANSACTION;                                    -- Oracle: omit
UPDATE u3_account SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE acc_no = 101;
CREATE TABLE u3_tmp (x INT);                          -- Oracle: x NUMBER
ROLLBACK;
SELECT balance FROM u3_account WHERE acc_no = 101;    -- 9900, NOT 10000
Expected: 9900. DDL commits the open transaction implicitly in both databases, so the debit was already committed before ROLLBACK, which then had nothing to undo. Clean up with DROP TABLE u3_tmp; and restore 101 to 10,000.
U3-D-03Abrupt termination — where MySQL and Oracle differL3Executable

MySQL. A begins and debits 101 by 500. B runs KILL <A's connection id>;. Then B reads 101 and debits it by 100; A runs any statement.

SELECT balance FROM u3_account WHERE acc_no = 101;                 -- 10000
UPDATE u3_account SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE acc_no = 101;  -- does not block (once rollback finishes)
-- A: SELECT 1;  -- error such as 2006 "server has gone away" or 2013 "Lost connection"

Oracle. Debit 101 by 500 (uncommitted), then run an anonymous block that debits 102 by 100 and then debits 104 by 1,000 (violating chk_bal) with no exception handler.

SELECT acc_no, balance FROM u3_account WHERE acc_no IN (101,102);  -- 9500, 5000
ROLLBACK;
SELECT acc_no, balance FROM u3_account WHERE acc_no IN (101,102);  -- 10000, 5000
Key difference. MySQL's KILL rolls back the entire transaction of the killed session, so B reads 10000. In Oracle the failed block's own changes (the 102 debit) are undone, while the earlier statement outside the block stays pending until your ROLLBACK. Error text: ORA-02290 (shown with ORA-06512 for the block).
U3-D-04Observing write-ahead log activityL2Executable
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit';        -- 1 by default
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G                                  -- LOG section: Log sequence number N1
UPDATE u3_account SET balance = balance - 1 WHERE acc_no = 101; COMMIT;
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G                                  -- N2 > N1
START TRANSACTION; UPDATE u3_account SET balance = balance - 1 WHERE acc_no = 101; ROLLBACK;
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G                                  -- N3 ≥ N2
Expected. The flush variable is 1 and the log sequence number increases after the commit. After a rolled-back change it normally still increases, because InnoDB logs the change and its undo. Oracle: SELECT acc_no, balance, ORA_ROWSCN FROM u3_account; — ORA_ROWSCN for the block holding 101 is larger after the commit. By default it has block-level granularity, so rows in the same block may share a value. V$LOG views need privileges and are omitted.

D.2 — Manual recovery drills (the algorithms on paper)

U3-D-05 · U3-D-06Deferred vs immediate modification — the two basic drillsL1Manual

1 <T1,start>   2 <T1,A,150>   3 <T2,start>

4 <T2,start>  5 <T2,B,200,250>  6 <T2,C,300,350>   CRASH
UNDO list: T2. REDO list: T1. UNDO backward: entry 6 → C = 300; entry 5 → B = 200. REDO forward: entry 2 → A = 150. Final: A = 150, B = 200, C = 300.

Crash after 10 — A trace. The undo restores D = 400 (entry 8) then A = 110 (entry 10's old value, which is T1's committed value, not the original 100). Redo T1 sets A = 110 again, so A ends at 110.

Related (U3-D-16, crash during recovery — repeatability). Using the log of U3-D-08 up to entry 10 with disk state A = 120, B = 200, C = 330, D = 440: recovery undoes T3 and redoes T1 and T2, giving A = 110, B = 220, C = 330, D = 400 — 3 items differ from the crash disk state (A, B, D). Crashing again after the UNDO phase (disk A = 110, B = 200, C = 330, D = 400) and running recovery from scratch gives the same final state, as does starting from A = 110, B = 220, C = 330, D = 400. Undo and redo write absolute values, so repeating them does not change the result.

U3-D-09UNDO-only loggingL2Manual
Initial: A=5, B=6, C=7.  UNDO-only: every write reaches disk before its commit record.
1 <T1,start>  2 <T1,A,5>  3 <T2,start>  4 <T2,B,6>
5 <T1,commit> 6 <T3,start> 7 <T3,A,55>  8 <T2,C,7>   CRASH
Disk state at crash: A=59, B=66, C=77.
UNDO list: T2, T3 (T1 committed). Undo backward: entry 8 → C = 7; entry 7 → A = 55; entry 4 → B = 6. Final: A = 55, B = 6, C = 7. T1's committed A = 55 survives, and T3's A = 59 is reverted to 55 rather than 5 — the old value is taken from the log, not the original.
U3-D-10Checkpoint recovery — deferred modificationL3Manual
Initial: A=10, B=20, C=30, D=40, E=50.  Deferred modification.  Disk at crash: A=11, B=20, C=30, D=40, E=50.
1 <T1,start>  2 <T1,A,11>  3 <T1,commit>  4 <T2,start>  5 <T2,B,21>  6 <T3,start>  7 <T3,C,31>
8 <checkpoint {T2,T3}>  9 <T2,D,41>  10 <T2,commit>  11 <T4,start>  12 <T4,E,51>  13 <T3,A,12>  14 <T4,commit>   CRASH
REDO list: T2 (in the checkpoint list, committed) and T4 (started after, committed). Ignored: T1 (committed before the checkpoint) and T3 (never committed).
Redo scan starts at entry 4 (<T2,start>): T2 was active at the checkpoint and, under deferred modification, none of its writes are on disk, so its pre-checkpoint write at entry 5 must be redone.
Redo T2 → B = 21, D = 41; redo T4 → E = 51. Final: A = 11, B = 21, C = 30, D = 41, E = 51. T3's writes (C = 31, A = 12) are not applied.
U3-D-11Checkpoint recovery — immediate modificationL3Manual
Initial: A=100, B=200, C=300, D=400, E=500.
1 <T1,start>  2 <T1,A,100,150>  3 <T1,commit>  4 <T2,start>  5 <T2,B,200,250>  6 <T3,start>  7 <T3,C,300,350>
8 <checkpoint {T2,T3}>  9 <T2,B,250,260>  10 <T2,commit>  11 <T3,D,400,450>  12 <T4,start>  13 <T4,E,500,550>   CRASH
UNDO list: T3, T4. REDO list: T2. Ignored: T1 (committed before the checkpoint, A = 150 already on disk).
Undo in order: entry 13 → E = 500; entry 11 → D = 400; entry 7 → C = 300. Scan limit: the backward scan must continue to entry 6 (<T3,start>), the earliest start record among the undo list (T4's start is entry 12).
Redo T2: entry 5 sets B = 250, then entry 9 sets B = 260. Redoing from the checkpoint onward gives the same B, because redo is idempotent and the checkpoint already flushed B = 250. Final: A = 150, B = 260, C = 300, D = 400, E = 500.
U3-D-13Rollback with compensation recordsL3Manual
Initial: A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4.  Immediate modification.
1 <T1,start>  2 <T2,start>  3 <T2,A,1,10>  4 <T1,B,2,20>  5 <T3,start>
6 <T2,C,3,30> 7 <T3,D,4,40> 8 <T2,A,10,100>  9 T2 FAILS (transaction failure, no crash)
(a) Rollback. Compensation records, backward: <T2,A,10>, <T2,C,3>, <T2,A,1>, then <T2,abort>. A trace: 100 → 10 → 1. T1 and T3 then commit → final A = 1, B = 20, C = 3, D = 40.
(b) Crash after <T2,C,3>. The redo pass repeats history (including the two compensation records). The undo pass finds T1, T2 and T3 without commit or abort. Undoing T2's entries again (A = 10, C = 3, A = 1) is harmless, because old values are absolute. T3's undo sets D = 4 and T1's undo sets B = 2. Final: A = 1, B = 2, C = 3, D = 4 (the initial state).

U3-D-15Immediate modification with an aborted transaction (tricky)L4Manual
Initial: A=10, B=20, C=30, D=40.
1 <T1,start>  2 <T1,A,10,20>  3 <T2,start>  4 <T2,B,20,25>  5 <T1,commit>

UNDO list: T3. REDO list: T1, T4. Ignored: T2 (aborted and already rolled back).
Undo backward: entry 10 → D = 40; entry 7 → A = 20. A is restored to 20, the old value in entry 7, which is T1's committed value (not 10).
Redo: T1 sets A = 20 (entry 2); T4 sets C = 40 (entry 12). Final: A = 20, B = 20, C = 40, D = 40. T2's B and C changes were already reverted when T2 aborted.

Related (U3-D-26, why UNDO must run backward). Initial A=1, B=5, C=9, D=0. UNDO: T1, T3; REDO: T2. Undo backward — entry 9 → D = 0, entry 6 → A = 2, entry 3 → B = 5, entry 2 → A = 1; redo entry 5 → C = 8 → A = 1, B = 5, C = 8, D = 0. Run forward instead and entry 6 would set A = 2 after entry 2 set A = 1, leaving A = 2 — wrong, since A was originally 1. The earliest old value must win.

U3-D-16Crash during recovery — UNDO/REDO is repeatableL4Manual

Uses the log of U3-D-08 up to entry 10 (T3 still active). Disk at crash #1: A = 120, B = 200, C = 330, D = 440.

Recovery 1. Undo T3, redo T1 and T2 → A = 110, B = 220, C = 330, D = 400. Compared with the disk at crash #1, 3 items differ (A, B, D).
Crash again after the UNDO phase, before any REDO. Disk at that moment: A = 110, B = 200, C = 330, D = 400. Recovery from scratch undoes T3 (A = 110, D = 400) and redoes T1 (A = 110, C = 330) and T2 (B = 220). Final: A = 110, B = 220, C = 330, D = 400 — the same.
Part 3, with disk A = 110, B = 220, C = 330, D = 400. The same recovery rewrites the same values → A = 110, B = 220, C = 330, D = 400. Undo and redo write absolute values, so repeating them does not change the result.
U3-D-17Shadow paging — page tables and the root pointerL2Manual

Shadow table: P1→L3, P2→L7, P3→L1, P4→L5, P5→L2. Free: L4, L6, L8, L9 (lowest free location is always used). Transaction T modifies P2, then P5, then P2 again.

Current table after T's writes:  P1→L3  P2→L4  P3→L1  P4→L5  P5→L6
  (P2 copied to L4 on its first modification; P5 copied to L6; the second P2 write is in place at L4)
CasePage table the database usesFree list
(a) crash before committhe shadow table: P1→L3, P2→L7, P3→L1, P4→L5, P5→L2L4, L6, L8, L9
(b) T commitsthe current table: P1→L3, P2→L4, P3→L1, P4→L5, P5→L6L2, L7, L8, L9
Crash before commit needs no undo — the current table is simply discarded and L4 and L6 are reclaimed. On commit the old locations L2 and L7 are freed.

U3-D-19Recoverability and recovery together (cascading dependency)L4Manual
Initial: A=10, B=20, C=30, D=40.  Immediate modification.
T2 computes B = A + 10 from T1's uncommitted A; T3 computes C = B + 10 from T2's uncommitted B.
1 <T1,start>  2 <T1,A,10,15>  3 <T2,start>  4 <T2,B,20,25>  5 <T3,start>
6 <T3,C,30,35> 7 <T4,start> 8 <T4,D,40,41> 9 <T4,commit> 10 <T2,commit>  CRASH (T1, T3 never commit)
Recovery. Undo T1 (A = 10, entry 2) and T3 (C = 30, entry 6); redo T2 (B = 25) and T4 (D = 41). Final: A = 10, B = 25, C = 30, D = 41.
Inconsistency. B = 25 was computed from A = 15, but A has reverted to 10. T2's committed effect derives from rolled-back data.
Classification. Not recoverable (T2 read from T1 and committed while T1 never committed); not cascadeless (T2 read T1's uncommitted A, and T3 read T2's uncommitted B); not strict.
Corrected state. If T2 had been forced to wait for T1, T2 could not commit, so T2 and T3 would also be undone → A = 10, B = 20, C = 30, D = 41 (only independent T4 survives).

Graph: the only shared item is B (w2(B) before r1(B) and w1(B)) → T2→T1; acyclic, serial order T2, T1. Classification: recoverable, cascadeless and strict — T1's read of B comes after c2.
